objetivo: By the end of this lesson, understand a short exchange, distinguish key German sounds from English, decode common spelling patterns and greet someone confidently.

blocos.texto: Your first mission: understand a conversation before memorising rules. Listen once without translations. Two people meet. Who asks how the other person is? How do they say goodbye? You will answer those questions in German before this session ends.

blocos.contexto: Anna and Ben meet on the street. Play the dialogue with English hidden; reveal it only after guessing the purpose of the exchange.

blocos.titulo: Five useful moves in a conversation
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: Open with «Hallo!» (Hello!). STEP 2: Ask «Wie geht’s?» (How are you?). STEP 3: Answer «Gut, danke!» (Fine, thanks!). STEP 4: Ask back with «Und dir?» (And you?). STEP 5: Close with «Tschüs!» (Bye!). Learn the phrases as a natural exchange; detailed grammar can wait. «Und dir?» is informal; for a formal conversation use «Und Ihnen?».
blocos.comparacao: English uses 'you' with almost everyone. German distinguishes informal dir and polite Ihnen; choose based on your relationship.

erros.errado: Gute Nacht! (as an answer to Wie geht’s?)
erros.motivo: Good night does not answer how someone is.
Use Ihnen for a formal exchange; dir is informal.

blocos.texto: English spelling is an unreliable guide to German pronunciation. Today you will stop reading German V, W, J and Z as if they were English. Your challenge: listen to two words, predict their first sounds, then correct yourself using the audio.

blocos.titulo: Four letter traps — and two new mouth positions
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: German W usually sounds /v/, as in English very: Wasser. STEP 2: V often sounds /f/, as in father: Vater; loanwords such as Vase may use /v/. STEP 3: J sounds /j/, the first sound in English yes: Jahr. STEP 4: Z sounds /ts/, like the end of English cats: Zeit. STEP 5: German S often sounds /z/ before a vowel at the beginning of a syllable, as in Sonne; in other positions it can sound /s/. STEP 6: To make Ü, position your tongue as for English ee and round the lips; Ö combines a front e-like tongue position with rounded lips. Neither is simply an English oo. Listen rather than trusting approximations.
blocos.comparacao: The most tempting mistake for an English speaker is to pronounce Wasser with an English /w/ and Vater with /v/. German often reverses those expectations.

erros.motivo: German w normally sounds like English v.

letras.som: Usually /f/ in native words; some loanwords have /v/
Like y in English yes, not j in jam

letras.som: Similar to the vowel in bed, but long and short forms vary

blocos.enunciado: Two-round pronunciation challenge. Round 1: say «Wasser, Vater, Jahr, Zeit» without using English letter names. Round 2: listen and imitate «Käse, Öl, Tür». Compare your mouth position with the audio; do not replace ö or ü with plain English vowels.

blocos.texto: Yesterday you learned that German letters do not always behave like English letters. Today you will become a word detective: look at a word, predict the sound of its letter combinations, then check your prediction against the audio. The win is decoding a new word without a phonetic crutch.

blocos.titulo: The four patterns that unlock dozens of words
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: German «ei» sounds /aɪ/, like eye: «Wein» and «Eis». STEP 2: German «ie» usually represents long /iː/, as in English see: «Bier» and «Brief». STEP 3: German «eu» and «äu» are pronounced /ɔʏ/, roughly like oy in boy: «Euro» and «Häuser». STEP 4: German «au» sounds /aʊ/, like ow in cow: «Haus» and «Auto». Now compare «Wein» and «Wien»: the spelling difference changes both sound and meaning. The patterns are reliable guides for these common words, not a promise that every letter group has only one pronunciation in every context.
blocos.comparacao: English speakers may see ei and say 'ee' or 'ay'. In German, start by trusting ei = eye and ie = ee. Train both directions: see the spelling and predict the sound; hear the sound and choose the spelling.

erros.motivo: Wien has ie /iː/; it means Vienna.

blocos.titulo: Consonant clusters you can read on sight
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: «sch» sounds /ʃ/ as in English ship: «Schule», «Fisch». STEP 2: «sp» and «st» at the beginning of a native German word or stressed stem normally start with /ʃp/ and /ʃt/: «Sport», «Stein». STEP 3: The two main sounds of «ch» are [ç] after front vowels (as in «ich») and [x] after back vowels (as in «Buch»). English has no exact everyday equivalent to [ç]; Scottish loch is a useful approximation for [x]. STEP 4: «tsch» sounds /tʃ/ as in English church: «Deutsch». STEP 5: «pf», «qu», «ck» and «ng» have their own patterns: «Apfel», «Quelle», «Jacke», «singen». Listen before trying to imitate unfamiliar sounds.
blocos.comparacao: English 'ch' in church is /tʃ/. German «ch» is usually [ç] or [x]; German «tsch» gives you the English church sound. Do not pronounce «ich» as English 'itch'.

erros.motivo: Initial sp in this German word is /ʃp/.

blocos.enunciado: Three-step decoding challenge. (1) Read «Wein» and «Wien» aloud and explain the meaning difference. (2) Read «Schule», «Sport», «Buch» and «ich» without transliteration; identify each consonant pattern. (3) Replay the audio and identify one sound you need to practise again. Say it three times, slowly then naturally.
blocos.exemplo: Wein /vaɪn/ = wine; Wien /viːn/ = Vienna; Schule /ʃ/; Sport /ʃp/; Buch [x]; ich [ç].

blocos.texto: Your final mission: navigate two real situations. First, you meet a friend in a café. Then you greet someone you do not know. You will choose a greeting, understand a short story, reply naturally and finish the conversation. At the end, you should be able to do this without English prompts.

blocos.contexto: First listen with English hidden. Anna and Ben know each other and speak informally. Notice how they ask a question back and how they end the exchange.

blocos.titulo: Choose the greeting and the register
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: For a friend, use «Hallo!» and «Wie geht’s?»; answer «Gut, danke! Und dir?». STEP 2: For a stranger or a formal setting, «Guten Tag!» and «Wie geht es Ihnen?» are useful polite options; you can ask back «Und Ihnen?». STEP 3: «Guten Morgen» is a morning greeting, «Guten Tag» a daytime greeting and «Guten Abend» an evening greeting. STEP 4: «Gute Nacht» is normally said when someone is going to bed, not as an evening arrival greeting. STEP 5: «Tschüs!» is an informal goodbye; «Auf Wiedersehen!» is a more formal farewell. German choices depend on the context, not simply the clock.
blocos.comparacao: English 'you' does not distinguish du and Sie. German does: «dir» with a friend, «Ihnen» in polite speech. Learn the right phrase for the situation before studying the grammar behind the pronoun endings.

tabela.german: Guten Tag! Wie geht es Ihnen?

erros.motivo: Use the evening greeting when arriving; good night is associated with going to sleep.
The polite form is Ihnen, not dir.

blocos.titulo: At the café — a short story you can now understand
blocos.ru: Guten Morgen! Anna ist im Café. Ben ist auch da. Anna sagt: Hallo, Ben! Wie geht’s? Ben sagt: Gut, danke! Und dir? Anna sagt: Auch gut, danke. Anna trinkt Tee. Ben trinkt Wasser. Das Café ist gut. Dann sagt Ben: Tschüs, Anna! Anna sagt: Tschüs, Ben!
blocos.pt: Good morning! Anna is at the café. Ben is there too. Anna says: Hi, Ben! How are you? Ben says: Fine, thanks! And you? Anna says: Also fine, thanks. Anna drinks tea. Ben drinks water. The café is good. Then Ben says: Bye, Anna! Anna says: Bye, Ben!

perguntas.resposta: At a café. The clue is «im Café».

perguntas.pergunta: Who drinks tea, and who drinks water?
perguntas.resposta: Anna drinks tea («Tee»). Ben drinks water («Wasser»). You can infer both from the familiar words.

perguntas.pergunta: What do they say when leaving?

blocos.enunciado: Capstone: perform two conversations, first with a friend and then formally with a stranger. With the friend: «Hallo! Wie geht’s? — Gut, danke! Und dir? — Auch gut, danke. Tschüs!». Formally: «Guten Tag! Wie geht es Ihnen? — Gut, danke! Und Ihnen?». Check whether you adjusted the greeting, question and ending to the person.
